## Introduction

<!--[No abstract is needed.]  Each replication project will have a straightforward, no frills report of the study and results.  These reports will be publicly available as supplementary material for the aggregate report(s) of the project as a whole.  Also, to maximize project integrity, the intro and methods will be written and critiqued in advance of data collection.  Introductions can be just 1-2 paragraphs clarifying the main idea of the original study, the target finding for replication, and any other essential information. You will likely contact the authors of the original study, so this should be professional and forward facing. It will NOT have a literature review -- that is in the original publication. You can write both the introduction and the methods in past tense.  -->

The experiment I have chosen was conducted by Lee and Gelman (2022) to investigate whether, for children and adults, behaviors that are seen as violations of property rights when referring to physical property are similarly viewed as violations when referring to digital property. Since data will be collected via SONA, I am proposing replicating only the adult sample from this study. In this experiment, adults and children rated how okay/not okay the actions of a character were after hearing stories about a person who downloaded a digital file that did not belong to them versus a person who took a physical item that did not belong to them. I am focusing on the result that adults found downloading a digital item to be more acceptable than taking a physical item (children’s pattern of evaluations looked very similar to adults’); the authors tested this finding using a linear mixed model. They found a significant main effect of format type, LRT, 𝛘2(1) = 194.2, b= -1.46, SE = 0.09, p \<.001. The authors also conducted one-sample t tests (two-tailed) to test whether participants' ratings differed significantly from a neutral valence (0); I will also replicate this test with my data. They found that adults rated taking a physical item negatively when compared to neutral, t(179) = -19.74, p\<.001, and rated taking a digital item neutrally, t(179) = 1.62, p \>.10. I have run their code and successfully reproduce these numbers using their data.

Additionally, since SONA studies must be 30 minutes, I am also going to ask participants an open ended question justifying their choice. This was included in the original study (“What made you think so? Describe your reason below.”), and the coding scheme the authors used is included in the paper.

This experiment is relevant to my own research interests as I have recently been interested in the development of children’s understanding of digital technology - specifically, I have been thinking about children’s thinking about their own digital privacy/ownership of their digital image in regard to their parents/caregivers sharing recordings of them. Understanding how people understand digital technology as similar or different to non-digital examples is relevant to this line of research. To this end, I may also try to increase my study length by adding an exploratory question(s) probing participants’ attitudes towards the sharing of their digital image via video recordings (maybe thinking of their own parents).

All data and protocols are available at <https://osf.io/3g2j4/>, including example stimuli. Adults in this study were presented with six scenarios, randomly presented via Qualtrics, in which a target character either placed a physical item left next to a shared computer into their bag, or downloaded a file from a shared computer onto their own. Participants responded how okay or not okay the action was using a 5-point Likert scale. Three of the scenarios adults read were about physical objects and three were about digital objects (music, movie, book, photo of nature, drawing, and game; the types of items shown in a digital versus physical format were counterbalanced).

Since the stimuli used in this experiment were written vignettes presented via Qualtrics, I am wondering now if this procedure will still lend itself well to coding a javascript experiment, since that is something I would like to gain experience with. I also see a potential challenge with replicating the stimuli and procedures exactly, since only one example of stimuli is posted on OSF and the authors counterbalanced the presentation of certain vignettes in a way that is slightly opaque to me. I anticipate that I may have to reach out to the authors for their full procedure and materials, or recreate them myself. Another challenge I foresee is that my sample may differ from the original study’s sample. The original sample consisted of adult participants recruited via Amazon MTurk in 2019. It is likely that the attitudes of undergraduates in 2026 may differ from those of general adults in 2019, particularly when it comes to anything related to digital technology.

Learning goals: By doing this project, I hope to learn how to run an experiment with human participants on SONA, as well as coding a javascript experiment. This project will also help me acquire skills in data analysis, specifically wrangling/cleaning data in R and running a linear mixed model (which I have pretty limited experience with).

Link to repository: <https://github.com/mikkahoffman/lee2022.git> Link to paper: <https://github.com/mikkahoffman/lee2022/blob/b99ec0bc5b82c91a985fb262e186f7811e3d0c25/original_paper/Lee%26Gelman_2022.pdf>

## Methods

### Power Analysis

Original effect size, power analysis for samples to achieve 80%, 90%, 95% power to detect that effect size. Considerations of feasibility for selecting planned sample size.

### Planned Sample

<!--Planned sample size and/or termination rule, sampling frame, known demographics if any, preselection rules if any.-->

The planned sample size is 60 adult participants. As the sample will be collected via SONA, participants will be predominantly undergraduate students, age 18-22.

### Materials

<!--All materials - can quote directly from original article - just put the text in quotations and note that this was followed precisely. Or, quote directly and just point out exceptions to what was described in the original article. --> 

"Adults read six scenarios in total (music, movie, book, photo of nature, drawing, and game) in orders randomized by Qualtrics, with three items presented in a digital format and the other three items presented in a physical format. In addition, the types of items shown in a digital versus physical format were counterbalanced." For example, for digital format scenarios, participants will read, "[X] finds that a book was saved on a shared computer in the room. [X] is the only person in the room. No one will know if [X] downloads the book on her computer. Is it okay or not okay for [X] to download the book on her computer? How okay or not okay is it?” In the physical version, the story is identical except that the item is shown as a physical object (e.g., "[X] finds that a book was left next to a shared computer in the room. [X] is the only person in the room. No one will know if [X] puts the book in her bag. Is it okay or not okay for [X] to put the book in her bag? How okay or not okay is it?”). In the original study, stimuli were presented and randomized by Qualtrics; in this study, stimuli will be presented and randomized via a web-based JsPsych experiment. 

I will also add in two additional new vignettes that will be similarly counterbalanced for format and randomly presented (so participants in this study will see 8 vignettes in total). These new items will be a photograph of a preschool-age child and a photograph of an adult (to probe ideas of digital privacy for children versus adults).  

### Procedure

<!-- Can quote directly from original article - just put the text in quotations and note that this was followed precisely. Or, quote directly and just point out exceptions to what was described in the original article. --> 

After providing informed consent, participants will see eight stories presented in random order. After reading each story, they will rate how okay or not okay the action was on a 5-point Likert scale with corresponding thumbs up/thumbs down images ("from -2 being totally not okay to +2 being totally okay"). They will also answer an open-ended question explaining each of their answers (“What made you think so? Describe your reason below.”). 

### Analysis Plan

<!-- Can also quote directly, though it is less often spelled out effectively for an analysis strategy section. The key is to report an analysis strategy that is as close to the original - data cleaning rules, data exclusion rules, covariates, etc. - as possible. --> 

Following the exclusion criteria from the original study, participants will be excluded if they do not complete all types of scenarios, or if their IP address is not based in the U.S. 

"Answers to open-ended questions from all 60 adult participants were also coded by two independent coders" - in this study, open-ended questions will likely be coded by one coder (me) due to resource constraints. "We predetermined the categories for coding explanations based on pilot testing with adults." Coding categories are specified in Table 1 of the original paper and will be used to code open-ended questions in this study. 

Raw data will be cleaned to remove identifiable and irrelevant data and will yield a clean tidy data file for adult ratings with subject ID, item, format type, and response (coded -2 to 2) as columns, and a .csv for adult explanations with columns for subject ID, item, format type, coding category, answer text, and coding (1 or 0 to indicate if the response was coded as including that coding category) - subject IDs will be repeated in this data frame as each subject will appear once in each coding category. 

**Clarify key analysis of interest here**  The key analysis of interest is the main effect of format type in the linear mixed model. 

"All statistical analyses were conducted with R statistical software (R Version 4.1.1; R Core Team, 2021). We analyzed ratings with a linear mixed model (LMM) using the R package ‘‘lme4” (Bates et al., 2015) and analyzed justifications with a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) using the R package ‘‘glmmTMB” (Brooks et al., 2017). Our full LMMs on ratings included format type, item type, children’s age in months [not relevant for this study], and all interactions among the variables as fixed effects and participant identity (ID) as a random effect. Our full GLMMs on justification included format type, coding category, and the interaction between the variables as fixed effects and participant ID as a random effect. We first compared the full model with a null model that included only participant ID as a random intercept. If the full model provided a significantly better fit to the data than the null model, we then conducted hypothesis-driven tests to examine the role of individual predictors by sequentially dropping them from the full model and assessed changes in model fit using likelihood ratio tests (LRTs)." 

To replicate the original analyses, these analyses will be run just on the original 6 vignettes. 

Additional analyses: I will also conduct follow-up one-sample t tests (two-tailed) "to examine whether ratings differed significantly from a neutral valence of 0." I also will analyze the justifications provided using the plan detailed above. I will also repeat the analyses detailed above with the full 8 vignettes to explore the effect of the two new vignettes. 

### Differences from Original Study

<!-- Explicitly describe known differences in sample, setting, procedure, and analysis plan from original study. The goal, of course, is to minimize those differences, but differences will inevitably occur. Also, note whether such differences are anticipated to make a difference based on claims in the original article or subsequent published research on the conditions for obtaining the effect. --> 

Differences in sample: The original sample was collected from adults ("M = 37.7 years, range = 24–66; 23 female and 37 male") on Amazon Mechanical Turk in 2019. This sample will be collected from undergraduate adults in 2026. Likely these samples will be different, as the age range of my sample will likely be narrower and younger, and there may be generational differences between these two samples. Their experiences with technology may be different, potentially leading to differences in their responses. 

Differences in procedure: The original experiment was presented, randomized, and collected via Qualtrics. In this study, I will present, randomize, and collect data via a JsPsych experiment that I code. While I do not anticipate this creating meaningful differences in participants' experiences, there may be differences in things such as font size, scale presentation, etc. As it is unclear if adults saw the same thumbs up/thumbs down Likert scale that children did, it is possible that my Likert scale presentation will differ from the original procedure. 

Differences in analysis plan: Although I am following the analysis plan laid out in the original study, it is possible that this analysis plan will introduce differences in my data. Specifically, as the original study was collected before generative AI tools were widely used, they did not account for screening out potentially AI generated answers in their data cleaning. By using their methods, I similarly will not be screening out potential AI answers - this could introduce poor-quality data into my sample. However, I think that potential AI data is less likely to be present on SONA, so I feel comfortable not including robust AI checks in my procedure.
